changes.summary: In April 1945, Gare d’Orsay train station became an arrival point for prisoners, deportees and workers requisitioned by the STO (Compulsory Labor Service) repatriated from Germany after the Second World War. Welcomed by volunteers and civil servants, they regained their administrative identities there before returning to their homes. Through a selection of previously unpublished documents, an exhibition sheds light on this significant episode, revealing personal stories at the heart of the nation’s history. From April 1945 onwards, former prisoners of war, political deportees from concentration and extermination camps and workers requisitioned by the Compulsory Labor Service returning home from Germany arrived on Quai d’Orsay by the truckload. Feted by the Parisians and sometimes awaited by anxious loved ones, they were directed inside the station by public administration officials and an army of volunteers. There, they went through the mandatory procedures that would enable them to return to civilian life a few hours later: an identity check, a wash and a shave, a medical checkup and lunch. Provided with a carte de rapatrié (repatriated person’s card), they could return to their home base if they still had one. Original objects (“auteur” photographs, contact sheets, correspondence, magazines and repatriated person’s cards), reproductions of images (negatives, posters and newspaper articles), a color film extract, and even a radio recording of the millionth repatriate’s voice … This is the first time that so many works and documents relating to this episode at Gare d’Orsay have been brought together and analyzed. The exhibition conjures up unique stories, each of which contains the whole of history, along with a wide range of viewpoints on these events that converge and sometimes oppose each other. This project, labelled by the National Mission for the 80th Anniversary of the Liberation, was made possible thanks to loans from the following institutions: The Heritage
